title: Agent Latency Alert on the Agent Stream
dataSources: Built-in Latency metric computed by Splunk Agent Observability from the traces in the Agent Stream; no evaluator is needed
description: Notifies the owning team when agent requests in a Splunk Agent Observability Agent Stream get slower than the agreed response time, using the built-in Latency alert.
value: Slow agents frustrate users before they fail outright. A latency alert tells the team while they can still find the slow model call or tool in the span tree.
implementation: On the Agent Stream's Alerts tab, add a Latency alert with aggregation max or average, a threshold set from the stream's normal range, and a window. Route it to the owning team by email, Slack incoming webhook or generic HTTP webhook.
visualization: Alerts tab history for the stream; Latency over time in the console.
knownFalsePositives: Long-running requests that are slow by design (for example report generation) raise the average. Put them in their own Agent Stream if their normal latency differs a lot.
detailedImplementation:
Prerequisites

A Splunk Agent Observability project for the application and one Agent Stream per environment or agent inside it. Do not create a second project for the same application: a second project splits the traces. The agent reads `SPLUNK_AO_PROJECT` and `SPLUNK_AO_AGENT_STREAM` from the environment. SaaS tenants authenticate with `SPLUNK_AO_REALM` and `SPLUNK_AO_O11Y_TOKEN`; on-prem tenants with `SPLUNK_AO_API_KEY` plus `SPLUNK_AO_CONSOLE_URL`. Install the SDK with `pip install splunk-ao` (`pip install "splunk-ao[langchain]"` for the LangChain callback).

Step 1 — Instrument the agent

The agent is already instrumented as described in UC-13.8.1: every request is a trace with at least one agent span, LLM spans carry `model`, token counts and the `tools` schemas, and tool spans carry `name`, `duration_ns` and `tool_call_id`.

Step 2 — Configure in Splunk Agent Observability

Open the Agent Stream, go to the Alerts tab and add an alert. Each alert is an evaluator or a built-in metric (Status Code, Cost, Latency, Trace Count), an aggregation (average, min, max, count or sum), a threshold and a window. Notifications go to email, a Slack incoming webhook or a generic HTTP webhook. Alerts never block a request. A generic HTTP webhook receives a body with `event` (`alert.triggered`), `conditions[].observed_value`, `dedup_key`, `deep_link` and any `metadata` configured on the webhook. Webhook auth is none, bearer or HTTP basic, and the credential is write-only after save.

Step 3 — Validate

Set a deliberately low threshold on a test stream, send a request, and confirm the notification arrives with a working `deep_link`. Then set the real threshold. This use case was written from the Splunk Agent Observability documentation without access to a tenant, so it ships as a draft. Confirm each step in the Splunk Agent Observability console before promoting it.

Step 4 — Operationalize

Write the threshold and window into the team's runbook next to the alert, and review them after the first month of alerts. Use the `deep_link` in the notification to open the traces behind it.

Step 5 — Troubleshooting

No notification: check the destination (email address, Slack incoming webhook URL, or webhook auth). Alert fires on every window: the threshold is inside the stream's normal latency range.

productArtifacts.title: Latency alert on the Agent Stream
productArtifacts.body:
Where: Agent Stream > Alerts tab > add alert
Metric: Latency
Aggregation: max or average
Condition: Latency above the agreed response-time target for the window
Window: match the team's response time; a shorter window alerts sooner and is noisier
Notification: email, Slack incoming webhook, or generic HTTP webhook
Notes: Use average for a general slowdown and max to catch single very slow requests.
